---
title: "Training load in the lactate zones"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

A step test gives the zones; training happens between tests. `training_load()` sorts the heart-rate, power or speed
samples of training sessions into the zones of `lactate_zones()` and answers two questions: how much time was spent
in each zone, and how was the training spread across the intensity domains?

## Zones from a test

The second test of the cyclist in `lactate_tests`, with LT1 at Log-log and LT2 at ModDmax:

```{r}
test <- subset(lactate_tests, test == "cycling_series_2")
results <- lactate_threshold(test, intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)
zones <- lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "ModDmax")
zones[c("zone", "domain", "intensity_from", "intensity_to", "heart_rate_from", "heart_rate_to")]
```

## Time in zone

Any data frame with one row per sample works: a CSV exported from a heart-rate monitor, a bike computer or a
training platform. Here is a made-up week of heart rate, one sample every 5 s:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
session <- function(name, minutes, heart_rate) {
  data.frame(session = name, heart_rate = round(stats::rnorm(minutes * 12, heart_rate, 3)))
}
week <- rbind(
  session("Mon easy", 90, 135),
  session("Tue intervals", 20, 140), session("Tue intervals", 24, 182), session("Tue intervals", 20, 140),
  session("Thu easy", 60, 138),
  session("Sat long", 240, 142),
  session("Sun tempo", 50, 165)
)
head(week)
```

Every sample counts for `interval` seconds in the zone of its value. With `.by`, each session gets its own row, in
the order the sessions appear:

```{r}
training_load(week, zones, interval = 5, .by = "session")
```

Without `.by`, the whole week is one row. The header says how the time was spread:

```{r}
load <- training_load(week, zones, interval = 5)
load
```

The plot shows the share of time in each zone, per session and for all of them, colored by domain like the zones:

```{r}
autoplot(training_load(week, zones, interval = 5, .by = "session"))
```

Five zones work the same way, and the distribution is still computed on the three domains:

```{r}
five <- lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "ModDmax", model = 5)
training_load(week, five, interval = 5)
```

## How the training was spread

The share of time in the moderate, heavy and severe domains is the training intensity distribution. Treff et al.
(2019) proposed a polarization index to tell the common distributions apart:

`polarization index = log10(moderate / heavy * severe * 100)`

with each domain as a fraction of the total time. A distribution is labeled:

* **polarized** when the index is above 2.00 and moderate > severe > heavy: much easy training, some hard, little in
  between;
* **pyramidal** when moderate > heavy > severe;
* **threshold** when the heavy domain holds the most time;
* **high intensity** when the severe domain holds the most time;
* **other** for anything else.

This week is pyramidal: `r round(load$zone_1_percent)`% moderate, `r round(load$zone_2_percent)`% heavy and
`r round(load$zone_3_percent)`% severe, with an index of `r load$polarization_index`. The distribution describes a
period of training, not one session, so give `training_load()` all the sessions of the period, for example with
`.by = "week"`. Treff et al. (2019) note that a threshold distribution can also be pyramidal; the label is a summary,
not a diagnosis.

## Heart rate or power?

Heart rate lags behind intensity: in short intervals it is still rising when the interval ends, so time in zone from
heart rate under-counts the highest zones (Seiler, 2010). Power or speed samples, with `measure = "intensity"`, do
not lag. Here is one interval session, 6 x (3 min at 330 W, 3 min at 150 W), with a heart rate that follows power
with a delay (simulated, with a time constant of 40 s):

```{r}
power <- rep(rep(c(330, 150), each = 36), times = 6)
stages <- test[test$intensity > 0, ]
steady <- stats::approx(stages$intensity, stages$heart_rate, power, rule = 2)$y
heart_rate <- numeric(length(power))
heart_rate[1] <- 110
for (k in seq_along(power)[-1]) {
  heart_rate[k] <- heart_rate[k - 1] + (steady[k] - heart_rate[k - 1]) * (1 - exp(-5 / 40))
}
intervals <- data.frame(power = power, heart_rate = round(heart_rate))

by_power <- training_load(intervals, zones, column = "power", measure = "intensity", interval = 5)
by_heart_rate <- training_load(intervals, zones, interval = 5)
data.frame(
  samples = c("power", "heart rate"),
  moderate = c(by_power$zone_1, by_heart_rate$zone_1),
  heavy = c(by_power$zone_2, by_heart_rate$zone_2),
  severe = c(by_power$zone_3, by_heart_rate$zone_3)
)
```

The power samples put `r by_power$zone_3` minutes in the severe domain; the heart rate only
`r by_heart_rate$zone_3`. When power or
speed is available, use it for interval sessions.

## Why time in zone, and not a training impulse?

Training impulse (TRIMP) scores multiply the time spent at each heart rate or in each zone by a weight and add it up
into one number. lactater reports the time in each zone instead: it is what the lactate zones measure directly, it
keeps the distribution that a single number hides, and it needs no weights from outside the test. If you need a
zone-based TRIMP, the minutes in each zone are what it is computed from.

polarized from non-polarized training intensity distributions. Front Physiol. 2019;10:707.
doi:10.3389/fphys.2019.00707
